areaOfRequirements: Security Compliance Throughout the Product Lifecycle

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (1) Article 13 (2) (3) (4)
content.hint: Before you build a product with digital elements, you need to think about security from the very beginning—during the design and planning phases. This means identifying what the product is supposed to do, how it might be used, how it might be misused, and what risks might arise from that. A cybersecurity risk analysis is a structured way of doing this: it helps you understand what could go wrong, how likely it is, and how serious the impact would be if it did. You should be able to show that you have specified security requirements early in the design process, and that these requirements were informed by a risk analysis. This analysis should be formally documented, meaning there is a written record that includes your reasoning, assumptions, and conclusions. It must also be kept up to date as the product evolves—when features change, when new threats emerge, or when it’s used in new ways. A proper risk analysis should also consider foreseeable misuse (for example, a customer using the product in a way you didn’t intend but that’s still likely) and the real-world environment where the product will operate (such as industrial networks, home Wi-Fi, or mobile apps). This broader context helps you design protections that are realistic and proportionate to the risk. Even if you’re a small team, the CRA expects you to do this kind of evaluation. You don’t need to follow a specific methodology, but your process must be clear, risk-based, and documented well enough to show that security was built into the product from the ground up.
content.genericTask: Conduct and maintain documented cybersecurity risk analysis from design through product lifecycle

content.requirement: Product is made available on the market without known exploitable vulnerabilities
content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, (1)(2b) Annex I, Part II, (1)(2)(3) Article 13( 5)(6)(8)(24)
content.hint: Under the CRA, your product must not be placed on the market if it contains known exploitable vulnerabilities. This means that before release, you need to check every part of your product—including third-party libraries and open-source components—for any published security issues. This is typically done using vulnerability databases (such as the European vulnerability database or NVD) and by analyzing your Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)—a detailed list of the components in your software. You should have a process to ensure that any vulnerabilities you identify are either fixed or addressed (e.g., by removing the component, applying a patch, or justifying why the risk is acceptable and mitigated). This process should be documented and proactive, not reactive. If a vulnerability is discovered after the product has been released, and it affects security in a meaningful way, you are expected to take immediate action—this could include issuing a security update or, in severe cases, pulling the product from the market until it is remediated. To support this, you should maintain an up-to-date SBOM in a widely used, machine-readable format (e.g., SPDX or CycloneDX). This helps you and others track what's inside your product and respond quickly when a new vulnerability is discovered in one of the components. The SBOM should be connected to your vulnerability management process so that whenever a new CVE or issue is reported, you can quickly check if you're affected and act accordingly. Ensuring your product is free of known exploitable vulnerabilities at the time it’s placed on the market is one of the core obligations under the CRA—and one of the clearest ways to demonstrate your commitment to cybersecurity.
content.genericTask: Verify absence of known vulnerabilities and integrate SBOM into release readiness and risk management

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (1)(2b) Annex I, Part II, (1)(2)(4) Article 13( 2)(3)(6)(8)
content.hint: Cybersecurity is not a one-time activity—it’s something that needs to be maintained over the entire life of your product. Continuous security testing means that you are regularly checking your product for weaknesses using techniques like static code analysis, dynamic testing, and penetration testing. You should be able to explain how often this testing happens (e.g., before every release, quarterly, or continuously using automated tools), and keep written records of the results. These records help you track improvements, identify trends, and demonstrate due diligence. If a vulnerability is found during internal testing, it should be handled just like a report from an external source—with formal tracking, classification by severity (such as Critical, Major, Medium, Low), and a clear plan for remediation. This means assigning responsibility, setting deadlines, and documenting what actions were taken or planned. Your security process should also cover third-party components. These can be a hidden source of risk if not properly monitored. You should have a routine in place to check for updates or security advisories related to the libraries or modules you use, and a method for evaluating whether updates need to be applied. This could be linked to your SBOM or vulnerability database checks. Ultimately, continuous testing isn’t about finding every possible problem—it’s about maintaining a consistent, structured approach to identifying and fixing security issues over time, so that your product stays safe and compliant as it evolves.
content.genericTask: Implement continuous security testing and vulnerability mitigation process with traceable records

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (c) Annex I, Part II, point (2) Annex I, Part II, point (8) Article 13, point 10 Article 13, point 11
content.hint: A secure update mechanism ensures that when you release a security update, it reaches your users safely, reliably, and in a way that they can trust. Your product should use a secure distribution system—for example, an encrypted update channel or a secure website—to deliver updates to users. This helps prevent attackers from intercepting or tampering with updates during transmission. All updates, especially security updates, should be cryptographically signed. This means they include a digital signature that users or devices can check to verify that the update really came from you and has not been changed. This is one of the key protections against malicious updates or fake patches. You should also have a clear internal policy to ensure that security updates are sent out without unnecessary delay once a vulnerability is confirmed. The Cyber Resilience Act also requires that these updates be provided free of charge, unless there is a specific contractual agreement that says otherwise. That means users shouldn’t have to pay extra to receive fixes for vulnerabilities in the product they already purchased. If you're not already doing this, it’s important to review your update process and make sure it includes signature verification, proper documentation, and timely delivery of fixes. These practices are essential not only for CRA compliance, but also for maintaining user trust and protecting your product in the long term.
content.genericTask: Deploy secure, signed update mechanism with timely and cost-free delivery policy

content.craReference: Article 10, point 12 Article 13, point 13 Article 13, point 14 Article 13, point 15 Article 13, point 16
content.hint: Under the CRA, you must define how long your product will receive cybersecurity support, such as security updates or vulnerability handling. This period—often called the support period—should reflect how long your product is expected to be used in practice and what a typical customer would reasonably assume. For many digital products, this is at least five years, but it can be shorter if the product clearly has a shorter lifecycle (for example, a disposable smart device or a limited-use system). You need to document this support period internally and make it publicly available to your users. Most importantly, customers must be clearly informed of the end date of support at the time of purchase—this means showing them, in an understandable way (like “Security updates will be provided until: June 2029”), when support will stop. This information should appear wherever the product is sold, whether online or in packaging, marketing materials, or user manuals. This transparency helps users make informed choices and prepares them for when they’ll need to upgrade or replace the product. It also helps you manage expectations and compliance. Keep in mind that if you shorten or change the support period after the product has been sold, that could raise legal and trust issues unless it’s already allowed under your sales terms or contracts.
content.genericTask: Define product support period and communicate end-of-support date clearly to users at purchase

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (b)
content.hint: “Secure by default” means that when your product is first turned on—without the user having to change any settings—it already uses the most secure configuration available. This includes things like requiring strong passwords, disabling unnecessary services or ports, and setting strict access controls. The idea is that even users who are not technical or security-aware are still protected because the product doesn't rely on them to make it secure. You should also ensure that if a user makes changes or something goes wrong, there’s an easy way to reset the product to a secure default state. This could be through a factory reset button, a software option, or a guided setup process. The reset should restore the original security settings—not just delete user data. These secure defaults help protect users from common mistakes, reduce the chance of misconfiguration, and make your product safer to use straight out of the box. It also shows that you’ve taken a proactive, user-friendly approach to cybersecurity, which is a key principle of the CRA.
content.genericTask: Ensure secure default configuration and provide reset option to original secure state

questions.questionText: Are your products set up with the most secure settings right out of the box, without the user needing to change anything?
Can users easily reset the product back to its original, secure state if needed?

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (c) Annex I, Part II, point (2) Annex I, Part II, point (8) Article 13, point 10 Article 13, point 11 Article 13, point 12
content.hint: Security updates are one of the most important tools for protecting your users and keeping your product compliant over time. Your product should be capable of receiving updates that fix vulnerabilities, and this should be possible through either automatic or manual methods. Automatic updates should be enabled by default, to protect users who might not otherwise take action—but users should still have the option to delay or opt out if they wish, as long as doing so doesn't compromise overall safety or compliance. Users must be kept informed about updates. That means when a new security update is available, the product should provide a clear notification that tells the user what the update is for, what it fixes, and what their options are. They should be able to install the update right away or choose to install it later. The user experience should make this process simple and understandable, even for people who are not technically skilled. In practice, your organization should also maintain an internal process for managing and distributing updates, ensuring that they’re tested, signed, and delivered securely. Keeping users updated in a timely and transparent way is not only essential for compliance—it’s a sign of quality and trustworthiness in today’s security-conscious market.
content.genericTask: Enable secure, user-aware update delivery with default automatic patching and opt-out options

questions.questionText: Can your products receive security updates to fix vulnerabilities, either automatically or manually?

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (e) Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (f)
content.hint: Access control refers to the ways your product prevents unauthorized users from gaining access to its features, data, or controls. You should have built-in safeguards like passwords, two-factor authentication (2FA), or role-based access controls (RBAC), depending on what is appropriate for the product and its users. These mechanisms make sure that only people with the right permissions can access sensitive parts of the system. Equally important is the ability to detect when someone tries to break in. Your product should include a way to monitor access attempts and generate alerts when suspicious or unauthorized activity is detected. For example, repeated failed login attempts, unusual access times, or attempts to bypass login mechanisms should trigger warnings. Having these protections helps prevent data breaches, misconfigurations, or malicious misuse. It also shows regulators and customers that your product takes the principle of “only the right person at the right time with the right access” seriously. Even simple products should include some form of basic access control and logging of unauthorized access attempts, with alerts if practical.
content.genericTask: Implement secure update capability with default automation, user notifications, and opt-out options

What is the mechanism to detect and alert on attempted or successful unauthorized access?

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (e)
content.hint: Data confidentiality means making sure that personal or sensitive data handled by your product cannot be accessed by unauthorized individuals. This applies to data stored on the product (like user credentials, configuration files, or personal settings) as well as data sent over networks (like cloud communication, app synchronization, or remote control signals). To protect stored data, you should use encryption or other technical controls such as access restrictions or secure storage modules. Encryption ensures that even if someone gets physical or remote access to the storage, they cannot read the data without the proper keys or credentials. For data in transit—when information is sent to or from the product—you should also use secure communication protocols, such as HTTPS, TLS, or secure APIs, to prevent it from being intercepted or altered during transmission. Even if your product only handles small amounts of data or doesn’t seem particularly sensitive, these protections are still required under the CRA. They help maintain trust with users and protect against data breaches, which can result in both regulatory penalties and reputational harm.
content.genericTask: Apply encryption and technical safeguards to protect sensitive data at rest and in transit

questions.questionText: How is personal and sensitive data stored on the product protected? Do you employ encryption or other technical means?
How is personal and sensitive data transmitted to and from the product protected? Do you employ encryption or other technical means?

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (f)
content.hint: Data integrity is about ensuring that the information used by your product—like settings, user data, commands, or software—cannot be changed accidentally or maliciously without permission. This means the product should include technical safeguards that prevent unauthorized modifications and verify that data has not been altered in an unintended way. You should have controls in place to restrict who can make changes, ensuring only the authorized user or system component can do so. Additionally, your product should be able to detect if something has been tampered with—for example, by using checksums, cryptographic signatures, or integrity verification mechanisms. If data corruption or unauthorized modification is detected, your product should be able to alert the user or log the event so that it can be investigated and fixed quickly. This protection is especially important for critical functions, configurations, or safety-related systems, where even small changes can lead to failures or security vulnerabilities. Demonstrating that your product protects and verifies the integrity of its data is a key part of CRA compliance and long-term product reliability.
content.genericTask: Implement controls to ensure data integrity and prevent unauthorized modification of stored and transmitted data

questions.questionText: Do you make sure that data, commands, software, and settings can’t be changed unless the user specifically allows it?
If data or configuration settings are corrupted or tampered with, how is this detected and notified?

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (g)
content.hint: Data minimization means that your product should only collect and use the minimum amount of data necessary to perform its intended functions—nothing more. This includes both personal data (like names, emails, or location) and technical data (such as device logs or usage statistics). If the product doesn’t truly need a certain piece of information to work properly, then it should not collect, store, or process it. You should review what data your product collects and why, and be able to justify each type of data as essential to the core function, performance, security, or user support of the product. This review should include checking default settings, third-party services, and built-in features that may be gathering information in the background. Limiting data collection not only improves privacy and helps meet CRA requirements, but it also reduces your responsibility for safeguarding data that’s not strictly necessary. Users are increasingly aware of how their data is handled, so being able to show that your product respects their privacy by design is both a legal and competitive advantage.
content.genericTask: Review and limit data collection to only what is necessary for product functionality

questions.questionText: Does your product only collect and process the data that adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for its intended function?

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (h)
content.hint: Availability and resilience refer to your product’s ability to keep working, even in the face of errors, attacks, or system failures. This is especially important for products that serve critical or always-on functions, like industrial devices, healthcare equipment, or smart home systems. Your product should be designed with built-in mechanisms that help it maintain its core functions during cybersecurity incidents or technical problems. This could include automatic recovery systems, failover components, watchdog timers, or fallback modes that allow basic operations to continue even if part of the system is affected. In addition, you should have protections in place against denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, which try to overwhelm the system with traffic or requests in order to shut it down. These safeguards might involve rate limiting, connection filtering, resource allocation management, or intrusion detection. Demonstrating that your product can resist and recover from disruptions is a critical part of showing compliance with the CRA. It also builds user trust—people expect that connected devices and services will be reliable, even when something goes wrong behind the scenes.
content.genericTask: Implement resilience features and safeguards to maintain core functionality during cyber incidents and DoS attacks

questions.questionText: Have you built in features that keep the product’s core functions running even during a cyber incident or system error?
Does the product include safeguards against denial-of-service (DoS) attacks or similar threats?

content.requirement: Impact on Other Devices or Networks
content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (i)
content.hint: Your product must be designed to coexist peacefully with other devices and networks it connects to. This means it should not generate excessive traffic, cause interference, or behave in ways that unintentionally affect the performance, security, or stability of other systems. For example, a connected device should not flood the local network with requests or monopolize bandwidth, and it shouldn’t trigger unintended behavior in other connected devices. You should be able to show that the product has been tested under normal and peak conditions to verify that it doesn’t disrupt other devices. This testing can include load testing, network simulations, or interoperability checks. If the product includes communication features (like Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or Ethernet), it’s important to ensure it handles connections efficiently and follows relevant protocols to prevent congestion or conflicts. These requirements are not just about being a good digital citizen—they’re essential for ensuring that your product integrates safely into the broader environment where it will operate, as expected by the CRA. This is particularly important for IoT or network-enabled devices that may operate in shared or critical infrastructure.
content.genericTask: Test and configure product to prevent disruption or performance degradation of connected devices and networks

questions.questionText: How do you ensure that the product operates without disrupting other devices or overloading the networks it connects to?
Have you tested the product to ensure it doesn’t unintentionally reduce the performance or reliability of connected systems?

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (b)(j)
content.hint: Attack surface reduction is about limiting the number of ways an attacker can interact with your product. Every interface, service, or feature that is exposed to users or networks could potentially be used to gain unauthorized access or exploit a vulnerability. To reduce this risk, your product should be designed so that only essential services and interfaces are enabled by default—everything else should be turned off, blocked, or removed. This means, for example, disabling unused ports, hiding debug or administrative interfaces, turning off test services before production, and removing any features not strictly needed for the product’s main function. You should also have a routine for reviewing the product’s configuration and functionality to make sure no new exposures are introduced over time, especially after updates or feature changes. Regularly reviewing and minimizing the exposed "attack surface" helps reduce the opportunities for cyberattacks and shows that your product follows secure-by-design principles. Even small actions, like closing unused ports or disabling unused wireless functions, can make a big difference in improving your product’s resilience against threats.
content.genericTask: Minimize and regularly review product attack surface by disabling unused interfaces and limiting exposed features

questions.questionText: Describe the measures implemented to reduce the number of ways an attacker could interact with or exploit your product, such as disabling unused interfaces?
Do you regularly review and limit exposed features, services, and ports?

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (h)(k)
content.hint: Incident impact reduction means building your product in a way that minimizes the damage if something does go wrong—like during a cyberattack, system failure, or unexpected behavior. Even with strong protections in place, incidents can happen. Your responsibility is to make sure that when they do, the effects are limited, controlled, and recoverable. This can include technical features such as isolating different parts of the system so that a compromise in one area doesn't spread, automatically restarting critical services if they crash, or using backup configurations that help the product recover quickly. It also involves setting up logging, alerts, and monitoring tools so that problems are noticed and addressed early—before they cause greater harm. For example, if a device is attacked with a denial-of-service (DoS) attempt, it should slow down gracefully rather than crashing completely. Or if an attacker gains access to a user account, access control mechanisms should prevent that account from changing core system settings. By thinking ahead and designing these kinds of protections into your product, you show that you’re not just trying to avoid incidents—but you’re also ready to respond and reduce their impact when they happen. That’s a key part of CRA compliance and a core principle of resilient product design.
content.genericTask: Implement exploit mitigations and damage containment strategies to limit incident impact

questions.questionText: If something goes wrong, are there built-in protections that help contain the damage and prevent further harm?
Describe techniques used to make exploiting vulnerabilities harder. Examples: sandboxing, memory protection, other mitigation methods.

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (j) (l)
content.hint: Activity logging and monitoring refer to your product’s ability to record important internal actions, such as changes to settings, user logins, software updates, or security-relevant events. These logs are essential for detecting and investigating security incidents, troubleshooting technical issues, and maintaining accountability over how the product is used. Your product should be able to store this activity information in a secure and tamper-resistant way, so that if something goes wrong, there’s a clear record of what happened. For example, if a setting was changed or a user logged in with administrative rights, it should be possible to trace that action in a log file or audit trail. While logging is important for security, it’s also necessary to consider user privacy. Users should be informed about what is being logged and why, and they should be able to opt out of non-essential tracking, especially if the logging involves personal data. However, for essential system operations—like security auditing or compliance-related events—opting out may not be appropriate or permitted under cybersecurity rules. In short, your product should strike a balance between robust internal monitoring and respect for user preferences, while always protecting the integrity of the logs themselves.
content.genericTask: Implement comprehensive activity logging with user options for opting out where appropriate

questions.questionText: Does your product keep track of important internal activities, like changes to data or settings, and can this activity be reviewed later?
Can users choose to opt out of this activity tracking if they want to?

content.craReference: Annex I, Part I, point (2), letter (k)(m)
content.hint: Secure data deletion and transfer are about giving users control over their personal information and ensuring that when data is no longer needed—or is being moved—it’s handled safely and responsibly. Your product should allow users to permanently erase all personal data and settings without requiring advanced technical knowledge. This is especially important when the product is sold, returned, recycled, or retired. Deletion should not simply remove the data from view—it should actually overwrite or erase it in a way that prevents recovery. For example, factory reset functions should fully clear user accounts, saved configurations, usage history, and any stored sensitive information. When users choose to transfer their data to another system, the process must be secure. This means the data should be encrypted during transmission and protected from unauthorized access. You should also provide clear guidance so users understand how to export their data safely and verify that it reaches the correct destination. These features not only help meet CRA requirements, but they also support privacy laws like the GDPR, and show users that you respect their right to control their data.
content.genericTask: Provide secure data deletion and protected data transfer capabilities for users

questions.questionText: Can users easily and permanently erase all personal data and settings from the product?
If users want to transfer their data to another product or system, can they do it securely without exposing sensitive information?

content.craReference: Article 13, point 13 Article 18, point 1 Article 18, point 3 Article 23, points 1 and 2
content.hint: Documentation and traceability are key administrative requirements under the CRA that help regulators, partners, and customers verify that your product meets essential cybersecurity obligations. You are required to keep the product’s technical documentation and the EU Declaration of Conformity on file for at least 10 years after the product is placed on the market—or longer, if the declared support period is longer than 10 years. These documents must be made available to market surveillance authorities if requested. Your product must also have a visible, legible, and traceable identifier—like a model number, serial number, batch ID, or another unique reference. If it’s not technically feasible to place this directly on the product (due to size or design), the information must be clearly provided on the packaging or in the accompanying documentation. In addition, you must provide users with either a full EU Declaration of Conformity or a simplified version that includes a direct link to the full version hosted online. This ensures that users, importers, and authorities can confirm that your product meets all the relevant legal requirements without needing to contact you directly. These measures help ensure accountability and make it easier to respond to issues like recalls, updates, or security incidents involving specific product versions.
content.genericTask: Ensure long-term availability of technical documentation and EU Declaration of Conformity, with clear product identification and accessible user information
